title: Green Party at a "crossroads", says former co-leader Adrian Ramsay
description: It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Members of the Green
body: It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Members of the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the policy motion last month. It led to a backlash from some Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including Ramsay and other Green MPs.Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski, who is Jewish, from entering the country.The Equality and Human Rights Commission also wrote to the Green Party asking for more information about the motion after concerns were raised by dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners.Labour later said it would end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disowned the policy. Speaking to Newscast, Ramsay replied "no, it's not" when asked if he thought Zionism is racist before adding he agreed with Polanski and others in believing that what is happening in Gaza is "appalling".The MP for Waveney Valley, who joined the party in 1998, said he does think Israel has a right to exist, something Polanski has stopped short of saying.Ramsay also said he has made it clear he is "deeply uncomfortable" with the motion adopted and suggested there is an "opportunity to take some action in relation to the motion in the run-up" to the party's spring conference next year.He said the question now is how Polanski and the party as a whole responds to the motion.Ramsay said: "I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment. "One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it - a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics."Ramsay said this is "perhaps seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties try to influence how those parties are run".He added: "What I want to see is the party really focus back in on our core aims as a party and our core values."Ramsay said this includes ensuring the party is "consensus-building in how we approach our politics" and that "we engage the grassroots of our membership".He added the party needs to be "very externally focused, because we're only going to be able to bring the environmental changes that we need to have to safeguard our society for now and for the future if the majority of the British public come behind that".Ramsay served as co-leader of the Greens from 2021 to 2025 alongside Carla Denyer, who is also now an MP.He unsuccessfully stood on a joint ticket with fellow MP Ellie Chowns in 2025, with the pair losing to Polanski in the leadership contest. Polanski, who missed the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, previously said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

schema.headline: Green Party at a "crossroads", says former co-leader Adrian Ramsay

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
description: Image source, Lisa ClewesImage caption, Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests ByYasmin RufoWhen
body: Image source, Lisa ClewesImage caption, Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests ByYasmin RufoWhen Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden."It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.Image source, Lisa ClewesImage caption, Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costsBut Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.Image source, AirbnbImage caption, The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins."We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal."It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".Image source, Krissi FoskettImage caption, Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay inDuring a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area."I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".Image source, Anthony MarshImage caption, Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb...Image source, Gasp image coImage caption, ... but will now list just two in light of the new rules He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals."It's common sense and common decency," he says.His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI, external.Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect."Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.Image source, Laura LewisImage caption, Laura Lewis says it's a matter of "basic respect" to wash dishes and take the bins outThe announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."Porsz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system."If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect."Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."Update 1 November - this article has been updated to remove a photograph of a contributor after they confirmed AI had been used in the image.

schema.headline: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

title: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
description: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final le
body: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."The King will make his speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said."You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK government's position".The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed. Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace."His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", external, and that Britain "must face up to the past".His pledge to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change."Institutions are under strain across the globe," said a Palace spokesperson. "The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua, they have attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island.

schema.headline: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology

title: Five teenagers stabbed at Halloween party in Chandler's Ford
description: Five teenagers have been seriously injured after being stabbed at a Halloween party, police have said.Officers were called to Park Road in Chandler's
body: Five teenagers have been seriously injured after being stabbed at a Halloween party, police have said.Officers were called to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, near Eastleigh, shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday.The injured teens - three boys aged 16 and two aged 17 - were taken to hospital.Hampshire Police said it believes an unknown group gained entry to a party at an address on Park Road before the stabbings.The force has appealed for witnesses and anyone with information to come forward.A police cordon remained in place on Sunday while officers continue their investigation.Senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie acknowledged the impact on local residents and thanked the community for its patience.Earlier, an eyewitness told the BBC ambulances and an air ambulance had attended.Another eyewitness said they saw someone running out of the house involved, shouting that he had been stabbed and that he was being chased by two people.

schema.headline: Five teenagers stabbed at Halloween party in Chandler's Ford

title: Ciara Mageean: European champion and Olympian dies aged 34
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mageean became a European champion in 2024Updated 6 hours agoFormer European champion and two-time Olympian C
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mageean became a European champion in 2024Updated 6 hours agoFormer European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34.Mageean, from Portaferry in Northern Ireland, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.She represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw from the 2024 Paris Games because of an Achilles injury.Earlier in 2024, Mageean had clinched the first major title of her career when she took 1500m gold at the European Championships in Rome.Prior to that she had also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning 1500m silver at Birmingham 2022.A statement posted on her social media on Sunday said: "At 6.30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones."A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed."Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam (may her soul rest in peace)."In a statement on social media, Athletics Ireland said: "We are heartbroken. An inspiration to so many, Ciara will be remembered for her courage, kindness and incredible spirit."Our deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and loved ones at this difficult time. Rest in peace, Ciara."In October, Mageean wed her long-term partner Thomas Moran in a small civil ceremony in Belfast.A talented athlete from a young age, Mageean played camogie for Portaferry GAC, but her dream of representing Ireland at the Olympics led her to pursue a career in athletics.Her running prowess was clear during an impressive junior career that yielded 1500m silvers at the 2010 World Junior Championships and 2011 European Junior Championships. She also reached the 2010 Commonwealth Games 1500m final as an 18-year-old. However, Mageean's early progress in the senior ranks was hampered by a serious ankle injury, which ended her hopes of making her Olympic debut at London 2012.Having had surgery in 2013, Mageean won the Irish 1500m title on her return in July 2014.In 2016, she claimed 1500m bronze at the European Championships in Amsterdam, but her Olympic debut ended in disappointment as she exited the 1500m competition at the semi-final stage.In late 2017, Mageean left her Dublin base to join Steve Vernon's Team New Balance in Manchester after parting ways with coach Jerry Kiernan.And while she endured some disappointing results following the move, Mageean claimed a European Indoor bronze medal in March 2019 before clocking two minutes 31.06 seconds to take 3.6 seconds off Sonia O'Sullivan's 27-year-old Irish 1,000m record at the 2020 Diamond League Monaco meet.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mageean won a gold medal at the 2024 European Championships in RomeMageean endured more Olympic heartache at the delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, when a calf injury disrupted her preparations as she exited from the heats.However, she enjoyed a successful 2022 campaign under the guidance of former Great Britain Olympian Helen Clitheroe, winning 1500m European and Commonwealth silver behind Laura Muir. Two weeks after the Euros, Mageean beat Muir and a world-class field to seal a stunning 1500m victory at Diamond League Brussels. Her time of 3:56.63 took 2.22 seconds off O'Sullivan's Irish record and marked her first sub four-minute run. In 2023, Mageean narrowly missed out on a World Championship medal as she finished fourth in a high-class final in Budapest. However, after taking over two seconds off O'Sullivan's Irish mile record in July, Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year.Figure caption, Ireland's Mageean takes 1500m gold as GB's Bell wins silverAfter a string of near-misses at championship level, Mageean secured the biggest win of her career at the 2024 European Championships in Rome. In a gripping final, Mageean found herself boxed in behind Great Britain duo Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie, but managed to dart through a gap and power down the straight to victory in 4:04.66.An ecstatic Mageean, who won admirers for her honest and emotional post-race interviews down the years, said "words can't even come close" to describing how she felt after sealing the first major title of her career.After Mageean's jubilation in Rome, injury again interrupted her Olympic bid as an Achilles injury forced her to withdraw on the eve of her heat in Paris.Earlier this year, Mageean said she was "continuing to find the joy in everyday" as she thanked people for their support following her diagnosis. Speaking to the BBC in June, she said she was "grateful" for having a career "that many others didn't get to have".

schema.headline: Ciara Mageean: European champion and Olympian dies aged 34

title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
description: Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in GermanyByJames ChaterUpdated 5 hours agoRioters looted shops in central Frankf
body: Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in GermanyByJames ChaterUpdated 5 hours agoRioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police detain a demonstrator dressed as Batman in FrankfurtOn Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended."We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.Image source, ReutersImage caption, People try to break through a window of a Frankfurt shop selling weaponsSimilar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations. In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind". A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe. In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.Figure caption, Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across EuropeFrench Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported, external that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

schema.headline: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent

title: How Harriet Dart revived career under former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli
description: In the hour following her first WTA title win, Britain's Harriet Dart had little time to respond to the stream of congratulatory messages flashing up
body: In the hour following her first WTA title win, Britain's Harriet Dart had little time to respond to the stream of congratulatory messages flashing up on her phone.Most pressing was making a call to her proud parents, Nick and Susie, who had been watching the final with friends at their local tennis club in north London, and her sister Phoebe. The next person she spoke to was 2013 Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli.Dart has been coached by the French former world number seven since the start of the season on a part-time basis, and she credits Bartoli for helping her achieve what some thought was beyond her.On Sunday, with Bartoli watching from home, the world number 115 won the Guangzhou Open in China by beating rising Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger."It's been quite incredible to work with Marion, and I was really fortunate she was open to working with me," Dart, 30, told BBC Sport in a video call from Guangzhou."I'm obviously at a very different stage of my career to someone who is, say, 20. But I still feel I have a lot to improve and there are gains to be made."She really believes in me - that means the world to me. Seeing a Grand Slam champion having that belief has made me believe a lot more in myself." When Dart started working with Bartoli, she was ranked outside the top 160. The pair live close to each other in Dubai and spend training blocks together there when Dart is not on the road.Dart and Bartoli, who has a young family, are not travelling full-time together on tour, but there have been opportunities for them to work on the ground, particularly during this year's Grand Slam tournaments.Dart says 42-year-old Bartoli still hitting the ball "really well" in practice is another benefit of the partnership.In Guangzhou, Dart was accompanied by her fitness trainer Dario Gonfiantini and boyfriend Stephen Falck. Without her coach, Dart had to largely rely on figuring things out herself - with the help of Bartoli sending over observational notes.Dart is projected to rise to 83rd on Monday after lifting the Guangzhou trophy to cap a stunning second half of the season.Dart has won 19 of her 24 tour-level matches on the hard courts since Wimbledon, taking her overall record on the WTA Tour this season to 23 victories from 34 matches - the highest winning percentage of her career."More than anything, Marion is just a great person. She cares about me as a person first and foremost, as well as improving me as a tennis player, of course," Dart said."It's been invaluable and amazing for her to share her experiences to make me better. "I've learned a lot from her and look forward to continuing to learn more. I hope we will be able to spend more weeks together next year."Dart reached a career high of 70th in the world in 2024, having made the Wimbledon third round and US Open second round, but has languished outside the top 100 for most of the past two seasons.During this period there have been clear vulnerabilities with her game, with opponents learning they could take advantage of a slow second serve that tended to produce double faults.There have also been questions about her on-court mentality and whether she could handle the pressure moments.In Guangzhou, she answered those doubts with a series of gutsy wins where she needed to fight back from behind."She's always had a fantastic work ethic and has always set the bar high with her professionalism," Anne Keothavong, Britain's women's team captain, told BBC Sport."But there is certainly more belief and confidence now. She's in a very good place."She's been grinding away on the tour for a long time and it's great to see someone who has put in a lot of time to succeed and win a big title."Keothavong named Dart in her squad for September's Billie Jean King Cup Finals and although she did not select Dart to play in the tie, she was impressed by her ball-striking during practice.Taking that level back on tour has helped Dart continue what has been an encouraging few weeks for British women in the Asian hard-court swing.Sonay Kartal reached the final of a WTA 1000 event in Wuhan, Katie Boulter made the semi-finals at a WTA 250 in Osaka and now Dart has won her maiden title at WTA 250 level.Last week, teenager Hannah Klugman won the biggest title of her career at the Wrexham Open - a W100 event on the second-tier Challenger tour."The way they're all performing towards the end of the season - at whatever level - has been impressive," added Keothavong."It's not easy at this time of the season because there has been a lot of tennis played, but they've all capitalised and risen to the occasion."It's great reward for all their hard work and is encouraging for British tennis."

schema.headline: How Harriet Dart revived career under former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli

title: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
description: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentiall
body: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise. In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.  Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour. In a BBC interview broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election. It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers. "There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said. "I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages.""I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling. The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come. The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week. But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year.""But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the "bulk" of spending cuts should be from the welfare budget, describing it as containing "astronomical sums".She also proposed reducing the size of the civil service and reducing budgets in departments such as the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.On whether she would support cuts pencilled in by the government, Badenoch told the same programme: "What exactly are they cutting? I'm not against what they're doing but there's no detail."Badenoch said she did not want to see cuts in frontline services but said there was a need to "bring down the cost of government".Reflecting on the Budget, she said: "The chancellor had 98 different measures, a lot of them very piecemeal, none will make a difference."So living within our means, absolutely, we've got to do that. That will require cuts to government, but we are setting out the things very clearly that we're going to change, the bulk of which is in welfare. Other departments will have changes too."

schema.headline: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers

title: Who will win the midterms? How the US elections will be won and lost
description: ByMike HillsVisual Journalism teamUpdated 30 October 2026Americans head to the polls on Tuesday to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency wi
body: ByMike HillsVisual Journalism teamUpdated 30 October 2026Americans head to the polls on Tuesday to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.Midterms come at bad time for TrumpOne of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.The battle for the HouseThe current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 18 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.Of those 18 toss-ups, 14 are currently held by Republicans and four by Democrats. But even if the Democrats didn't win any of them, they would still win the House if they take the 36 seats classed as likely or leaning Democratic.Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.The battle for the SenateThe Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.What are the key issues for voters?Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US.The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?Can Trump defy political gravity?Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.In mid-October, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had about $320m (£240m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $230m (£170m). On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $160m (£120m) held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement.The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising.More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact, external. Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups.Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party.Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Who will win the midterms? How the US elections will be won and lost

title: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash
description: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.D
body: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people. The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and  was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself."Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB". Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death."Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said."Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit. "Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.More than 540 people were on board both trains.The Foreign Office has been contacted by the BBC.

schema.headline: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash

title: Seven arrested after Birmingham city centre firework disorder
description: Seven people have been arrested after disorder, involving fireworks being set off, in a city centre. Footage posted on social media showed crowds gath
body: Seven people have been arrested after disorder, involving fireworks being set off, in a city centre. Footage posted on social media showed crowds gathered on Corporation Street in Birmingham, with fireworks being set off close to police officers and vehicles. West Midlands Police had warned firm action would be taken against anyone involved in fireworks-related disorder,  following serious incidents in the city during Bonfire Night last year. Those arrested, aged between 15 and 26, were held on suspicion of offences including assault, possession of fireworks and possession of an offensive weapon. They all remain in custody for questioning, the force said.Officers used Section 60 stop-and-search powers, which allow searches without the need to have reasonable grounds to do so. The arrests were made in and around Stephenson Street and Corporation Street, after officers responded to "pockets of disorder," involving fireworks being set off in a dangerous manner, said the force. Ch Supt Tom Boyce said: "Misusing fireworks is not only dangerous: it's illegal and can lead to fines, arrest and criminal charges."The force said extra officers had been deployed at key locations to prevent a repeat of last year's violence.On 6 November 2025, 21 people were arrested after officers were attacked with fireworks on Dale End and Staniforth Street.

schema.headline: Seven arrested after Birmingham city centre firework disorder

title: Women's Super League: Defeat for London City - but is Europe a real possibility?
description: It shows how quickly London City Lionesses have progressed that they were hugely disappointed with a narrow defeat by defending champions Manchester C
body: It shows how quickly London City Lionesses have progressed that they were hugely disappointed with a narrow defeat by defending champions Manchester City.For a team that were playing second-tier football 18 months ago, their lofty ambitions of qualifying for the Champions League suddenly don't seem farfetched.London City looked like the better team for most of the afternoon at Hayes Lane but were given a harsh lesson by the visitors in how to be ruthless.Manchester City needed goals from Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp against the run of play, but they dug in to win 2-1 and to continue setting the pace at the top.Those goals came after countless opportunities went begging for London City, who ended the game having had 24 shots but only six on target.The performance was enough, however, to show that London City are more than capable of competing with the WSL's elite. The next question, is whether they can do it consistently.London City Lionesses are a club who do things differently and, backed by US billionaire Michele Kang, they are not shy to disrupt the current order.They are an independent women's football club who have spent big in the transfer window and agreed a record-breaking shirt deal with Nike believed to be worth more than £3m a year.They have built their own training facility in Kent and persuaded superstars such as Alexia Putellas to join in the summer.Spain international Putellas showcased her latest Ballon d'Or trophy - the third of her career - before kick-off on Sunday.London City Lionesses are clearly no minnows, but even a squad full of superstars needs time to gel.It was for this reason that people doubted whether they were ready this season to qualify for the Champions League and break the WSL's traditional top three.But on Sunday's showing, they are not as far off as people thought.Manager Eder Maestre said the team's performances are already at the level they want but results have not always shown that and they still have work to do."That's why it's a very frustrating situation. We were speaking a lot about respecting the identity and it doesn't matter the team that we were facing," the Spaniard said. "The next step in that project was showing everybody that we can perform, while respecting that identity that we are trying to build on."That's why it's doubly frustrating, because I think the result was not the one we deserve. Manchester City are more mature. "They are more used to it. When you have this consistency and you are very used to playing these kinds of games, maybe you have more experience. "That's why we have extra nervousness in the moments that we need to be more clinical."Where London City fell was where Manchester City stood tall.Moments of brilliance by world-class players Shaw and Hemp delivered the goods and when London City's pressure grew, so too did Manchester City's resilience.It is that consistency across 90 minutes, and the season as a whole, that Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz believes will demonstrate the difference."They are a very good team and they really showed the highest level," said Jeglertz."What it means to be at the top of this league, is playing week after week, and at the same level - and finding different levels to win."That is what we have created. That's what everybody who wants to win something needs to be able to do. To contest, you need to compete for the whole season."London City Lionesses are providing plenty of optimism on the pitch but even if they were to qualify for the Champions League this season, are they allowed to?Current Uefa rules state that owners cannot have two clubs competing in the same competition meaning one of Kang's Lyon or London City Lionesses would miss out.It is a dilemma that many have discussed but if they continue to perform so well, it could prove to be a problem earlier than expected."First of all, what we feel is important, is to be part of the conversation," London City's chief executive officer Martin Semmens told BBC Sport. "The next stage is getting towards trophies. Our ambition is to be in Europe, to play in Europe every year, and to compete with the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal. "We're probably one step behind that in squad development and all the other things we have to do. But on our day, we feel we can beat them."London City's ambitions are clear - so what happens if they do qualify this season?"I think Michele [Kang] has a really clear view and that is that she wants to see as much investment come into the women's game as possible," added Semmens. "The men's multi-club ownership rules is about being careful not to have control over two clubs. We see it differently on the women's side."We want to see more investment, so we believe if you invest in more than one club, the game will accelerate faster. "We truly understand and respect the rules, always. But there are logical, structured ways that we can compete in Europe next season."

schema.headline: Women's Super League: Defeat for London City - but is Europe a real possibility?

title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate ra
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate racesByNorth America correspondent in Lubbock, TexasThe race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year – a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans."If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat. At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual."It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."Image source, ReutersWhen Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters – with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate."Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning – "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" – is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music.  He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state."A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump won Texas in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential electionsFor Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump – alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton – was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size."If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans."Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X. "When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia."I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser. "The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican candidate Ken Paxton has a Trump endorsement - and some past controversies in Texas politicsFor the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics – a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser."Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one. Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war. Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters – many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 – have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies. Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state – a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability."It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midtermsThen there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement."Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud – later dropped – and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges. The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics – and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midtermsIN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightropeTalarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas. Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race. Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state – spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries – two powerful interests in the state.Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.He frequently leans into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late – the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath."We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again."I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?

title: Celebrity Traitors: Why the real winners are Maya Jama, King Kenny and Miranda Hart
description: Image source, BBC/Studio LambertByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors finalIn som
body: Image source, BBC/Studio LambertByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors finalIn some ways, all the players on The Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.Miranda HartAfter a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment."Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun, external, the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.Image source, BBC/Studio LambertThe BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.And then there’s James Acaster, who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor, with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms. Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.King KennyWhen it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final.Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny."He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.Maya JamaFellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week, external.What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors."Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.Joanne McNallyOf all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final."And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.Just a few days ago, it was announced, external that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.As it happened: Relive the Celebrity Traitors finalCulture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes, when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men."There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.Sebastian 'Bash' CroftIn the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper, but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.And what's in store for the others...What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry.But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.And what of James Blunt, who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.

title: Henry Nowak: Southampton student’s family on police footage

body: Nowak family say police footage deepened traumaFigure caption, Dear Henry: Our Fight for Justice, a Tonight special, airs on Thursday, 5 November, at 21:00 on ITV, ITVX and ITV News YouTube channelUpdated 42 minutes agoThe family of Henry Nowak have said the trauma of learning he had been murdered was made worse by watching police footage of officers handcuffing him as he lay dying.They told ITV their "world has changed twice", first when they were told he had died, and again when they watched the body-worn camera video.His killer, Vickrum Digwa, falsely told police Henry had racially abused him, and officers handcuffed the student as he repeatedly said he had been stabbed.His father Mark, stepmother Katie, mother Lucy and sister Olivia were speaking to ITV for the documentary Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice.Image source, HandoutImage caption, Henry Nowak, 18, was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December 2025Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder, led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk, which will look at "any missed opportunities to intervene".Henry, 18, was stabbed five times as he walked home from a night out with friends from his football team in Southampton on 3 December 2025.Digwa, 23, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years.It took officers another 24 hours to identify Henry's body and tell his family."I jumped out of bed and I saw the police car on our driveway," said Katie."One of the police officers was holding his hat in his hand, and I just knew straight away that something horrific had happened."She said Mark fell to his knees when he heard the news."He let out a cry that I'll never forget," she said."I just remember saying 'it's Henry' and breaking down in tears," Mark said. "It's just unbelievable pain."Image source, ITV NewsImage caption, Mark Nowak fell to his knees after learning that his son Henry had been murderedOfficers went to Lucy's home at the same time. "We got that dreaded knock on the door at one o'clock in the morning," she said."They said to me, 'Do you have a son called Henry?… There's been an altercation. And unfortunately, your son has passed away'."No words, no words can explain that feeling."Olivia said she rang her father after hearing the news. "I just remember this scream. It was awful. He screamed 'My boy, my boy'," she said.She now keeps some of Henry's T-shirts on his bed and told ITV they still smell of him and give her comfort.But Lucy said she could no longer enter his bedroom because of the memories it holds."I can't go in there," she said.Coats now hang over the bedroom door so she does not have to look at it as she passes.Image source, ITV NewsImage caption, Olivia Nowak and Lucy Ross were told of Henry's death when police knocked on their door in the early hoursChalk said: "Serious questions have been raised about whether agencies and organisations failed to act on complaints about Digwa's violent and erratic behaviour."My review will follow the evidence without fear or favour. It will also examine how public authorities treated the Nowak family at a time of unimaginable pain."Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice, a Tonight special, airs on Thursday 5 November at 21:00 GMT on ITV, ITVX and the ITV News YouTube channel.Get in touchYour Voice
